articles.title: Russian director refuses to denounce lead actor despite criticism from Ukraine
articles.summary: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, about physicist Lev Landau, stars Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who has refused to speak out against Putin’s war. The director of a controversial new Russian film has said “everyone pays for his own choice” when asked about his lead’s refusal to condemn Russia’s war…
body: In film-maker Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, which premiered at the Venice film festival on Wednesday, Greek-Russian star conductor Teodor Currentzis plays the eponymously nicknamed protagonist, Nobel prize-winning quantum physicist Lev Landau.

In the run-up to the festival, the film’s inclusion in the lineup was heavily criticised by the Ukrainian ministry of foreign affairs, in part over the fact that Athens-born Currentzis continues to live and work in Russia, and has never publicly denounced Putin’s war.

“It’s his choice,” Khrzhanovsky said at a press conference on the Lido. “But I think everyone is paying for his own choice, his own life, his own destiny,” added the film-maker, who has renounced his Russian citizenship over the full-scale invasion and lives in exile in Germany.

He referred to his film, in which Currentzis’s character Landau is put under pressure to work on the development of the nuclear bomb and eventually reluctantly agrees. “As you can see in the movie, the main character is also making different choices, and he’s paying for his choices.”

articles.title: ‘Entourage’ Creator Slams ‘God-Awful’ Ad Reuniting Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier: A ‘S—ty Imitation’ That ‘Makes Me Puke’
articles.summary: “Entourage” creator Doug Ellin has spoken out against an ad reuniting Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier, calling it a “cheap, shitty imitation” of his beloved HBO comedy.
body: On Wednesday, Variety broke the news of Piven and Grenier’s on-screen reunion, which took place in a three-minute spot for Jake Paul’s gambling app Betr. Ellin said in a video message that he received “400 messages” about the “god-awful commercial,” clarifying that he was not involved in its creation.

Ellin said he’s not bitter over not being paid for the ad. He simply wishes the writers of “Entourage” would get more credit for the hard work they put into the scripts and character development, only for their work to be distilled into an “embarrassing” emulation of the HBO hit.

“I watch it and I want to throw up, because I would suffer, along with many other people, over every syllable, every fucking word,” Ellin said. “So I watch this trash, this shit, and go, ‘Ugh, ugh.’ There’s no bitterness. I want everyone to get paid, get rich. Just fucking do your own shit. That’s all.”

Ellin then seemed to take a shot at Piven — who won three Emmys for playing Ari on the series — claiming that the actor distanced himself from “Entourage” in the years following the 2011 series finale and 2015 movie.

articles.title: Union Town review – passionate exposé of US delivery workers’ employment conditions
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Barbara Kopple returns with her third film investigating US workers’ rights – this time, undocumented ‘deliveristas’ and the attempts to unionise Amazon staff.
body: Barbara Kopple’s documentary about app-based delivery workers is a stirring, defiant, battle-hardened affair, swinging between the fraught picket line and the still more hazardous New York City streets. It’s a new film that feels old in the best sense of the word; a hoarse battle cry that summons the ghosts of The Grapes of Wrath and the New Deal, Eugene Debs and Woody Guthrie. That America is long dead and buried, a casualty of changing times, but Kopple sees no reason why it should not rise again.

articles.summary: Chernin Entertainment, the prolific independent film and TV producer founded by former News Corp. chairman Peter Chernin, has expanded its in-house film team. Under movies chief David Ready, the film unit has had big wins this year in theaters (“Backrooms”) and on streaming (Netflix’s “The Last…
body: Meanwhile, Samantha Nisenboim has been named senior vice president of film. Her producer credits include “The Lego Batman Movie,” The Tomorrow War” and “Renfield.” She is currently producing two feature films at Chernin, including the Netflix thriller “The Big Fix” starring Mark Wahlberg and Riz Ahmed.

Finally, Max Gains has been named creative executive. He began his career at Paramount before joining 21 Laps, where he spent six years working his way up from Shawn Levy’s assistant. His projects included “Deadpool & Wolverine,” “The Adam Project” and “Free Guy.”

Ready told Variety that the company has “built a strong foundation and a slate we really believe in, and now we have the team to build out our next chapter. Marisa, Brady, Samantha, and Max are the kind of executives you want on your team – smart, relentless, deeply connected and driven by great material.”

Chernin recently inked a new multi-year, first-look feature film deal with Apple Studios. In January, Mediawan announced an agreement to acquire Chernin parent The North Road Company. articles.title: John Malkovich cancels Israel trip over fabricated solidarity quote
articles.summary: The Wild Horse Nine actor had been due to appear on stage in The Music Critic in Tel Aviv – but pulled out over PR firm’s ‘unacceptable and untenable’ attribution of statement.
body: John Malkovich has cancelled a planned trip to Israel next year to appear on stage after a PR firm hired by the show attributed quotes to the actor that the company had written.

Malkovich, who is a leading Oscar contender for his role in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, was due to appear in The Music Critic, a theatrical-musical satire composed by the Jewish violinist Aleksey Igudesman, in Tel Aviv’s Charles Bronfman Auditorium on 13 April.

A press release circulated on 5 September quoted Malkovich as saying he was “thrilled to return to Israel” and looked “forward to meeting the warm Israeli audience once again, to whom I feel a strong closeness and solidarity”.

The actor, 72, was alerted to the quotes after reading them in the Hollywood Reporter, who picked them up from the Jerusalem Post. In a statement to the Hollywood Reporter on 8 September, Malkovich said that a “PR company hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed.”

articles.title: Axios Co-Founders Urge Wielding AI to Help ‘Simplify’ Your Life in New Book
articles.summary: The co-founders of Axios popularized the “Smart Brevity” mantra for years. Now, in the age of AI, comes another: “Simplify.” Such is the name of a new book by Mike Allen, Jim VandeHei and Roy Schwartz, who co-founded the political news site in 2016 to try and help get people smarter faster.
body: AI is as much a character in the book as any of the co-founders or the company itself, reflecting Axios’ ethos that the technology will be a “moonshot” for its growth (a sentiment that came days after it laid off 11 staffers in March). The company’s enthusiastic adoption of the technology has also made its way into several columns written by VandeHei and Allen, along with a post written by publisher Nick Johnston that drew some mockery over his admission that he used AI as a guide while reading “The Last of the Mohicans.”

“I don’t have a lot of friends that are reading the classics at the beach,” Allen says in his defense, urging people to read the piece. “Nick is an actual book reader, and he’s someone who’s reading James Fenimore Cooper, reading ‘The Last of the Mohicans,’ reading, on paper, in hardcover, a classic, and he’s using AI as a smart friend to talk about it as he went along.”

articles.title: The Uprising review – the peasants are revolting in muddled historical epic
articles.summary: Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period piece. Hollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them.
body: On paper, The Uprising should be different: it’s a historical epic from a blue-chip director (the Bourne trilogy’s Paul Greengrass ), a nuanced, introspective leading man ( Andrew Garfield ) and a milieu that uncomfortably chimes with the western world’s backslide into repressive authoritarianism (The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381). In reality, it is a disjointed slog through the mud with the emotional depth of a History Channel rerun.

Thus follows a rather hectic-feeling race from one greige setting to the next as the rebels have their run of modern-day Kent, assembling in Maidstone before storming Canterbury cathedral, and then traveling to meet the king and his men in Blackheath. Greengrass’s camerawork can occasionally swoon, with stunning aerial shots of a flotilla on the Thames, but his signature handheld style is a trick that has gone stale: the only uprising I felt during the seasick fight scenes was my breakfast threatening to return on me.
points: Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period piece.
Hollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them.

articles.title: BBC drops Drag Race UK after eight series
articles.summary: Future series will no longer be broadcast on BBC Three as the show moves to a streaming platform owned by its production company.
body: RuPaul's Drag Race UK is leaving the BBC after eight series, the broadcaster has confirmed.
A spokesperson for the channel said it was facing "very difficult choices" in the face of "significant financial pressures".

The show is currently broadcast on BBC Three and iPlayer. Future series - as well as its spin-off vs The World - will be broadcast on Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.
At its peak, the UK version of the international drag competition averaged at around 1.5 million viewers per episode.

articles.title: Your Favorite Hollywood Hotspot? Guess Who Owns It.
articles.summary: A billionaire Abu Dhabi royal has been snapping up Hollywood watering holes like they’re going out of style. But two LA hangouts – the Sunset Tower and the San Vicente Bungalows – just turned down a $700M offer.
body: What do Annabel’s, Sexy Fish, Delilah and the Bird Streets Club have in common — besides serving as Leonardo DiCaprio’s natural habitat? They’re all now controlled by investment interests tied to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Abu Dhabi royal who has been snapping up trophy properties across L.A. — and whose acquisition spree recently sparked rumors up and down the strip that the Sunset Tower Hotel and Jeff Klein’s San Vicente clubs might be next.

Tahnoon isn’t merely some fabulously rich dude who woke up one morning with a taste for bottle service. In addition to assembling a sizable collection of the world’s most celebrity-clogged watering holes, he happens to be the UAE president’s brother, the country’s national security adviser and deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi. His investment universe extends well beyond IHC: He also chairs the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and AI giant G42.

But the sheikh must really love a red velvet rope because apparently his nightlife shopping spree isn’t over. According to a source familiar with the discussions, DIAFA recently approached Klein about buying the Sunset Tower and his San Vicente clubs for the princely sum of $700 million.
points: A billionaire Abu Dhabi royal has been snapping up Hollywood watering holes like they’re going out of style.
But two LA hangouts – the Sunset Tower and the San Vicente Bungalows – just turned down a $700M offer.

articles.title: ‘Survivor 51’ Cast Reveals What They’re Trying to Hide (Exclusive)
articles.summary: "The bigger of an idiot I am, the better my game" is just one of 21 revealing answers about what the new cast hopes nobody notices when the reality competition returns.
body: Okay, that’s not exactly breaking news. Deception has been part of the game ever since Richard Hatch convinced Rudy Boesch to form the show’s first alliance 26 years ago. Contestants deceive each other over alliances, advantages, idols and votes so often that “tell a convincing lie” could be item No. 1 on every Survivor player’s to-do list.

When The Hollywood Reporter visited set and asked each member of the cast, “What’s something about you or your game that you’re trying to keep under wraps heading into the season?” a clear pattern emerged. Whether they’re concealing a law degree, downplaying a successful career, disguising their personality or masking parts of their personal lives, nearly everyone is trying to accomplish the same thing: control how they’re perceived before the game even begins.
For some members of the Survivor 51 cast, the game begins with a simple rule: Don’t tell people what you really do for a living.
Patt doesn’t hesitate when asked what she’ll keep under wraps. “I’m an attorney, I got to lie. You have to lie about being an attorney. It’s just the number-one rule.”
